value.overview: The Broad-winged Hawk is a medium-sized forest hawk that breeds across much of eastern North America and migrates to Central and South America. It is famous for forming large, swirling flocks called kettles during migration. In Costa Rica, it is primarily a common migrant and winter visitor rather than a breeding species. It often uses forest edges, open countryside, hillsides, and other areas where trees provide hunting perches and nearby clearings provide access to prey.
value.classification: The Broad-winged Hawk belongs to the order Accipitriformes and the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae. Its scientific name is Buteo platypterus.
value.identification: This stocky hawk has broad, rounded wings, a relatively short tail, and a large head. Adults usually show dark upperparts, pale underparts with fine barring, and a boldly banded tail with black and white bands. The dark trailing edge of the wings is noticeable in flight. Juveniles are browner and more heavily streaked below, with a banded tail. Its call is a high, thin, two-part whistle. Migrating birds are often identified in large soaring groups.
value.rangeHabitat: Broad-winged Hawks breed in deciduous and mixed forests of eastern and central North America, usually near forest openings, wetlands, or other clearings. They winter from southern Mexico through Central America into northern and central South America. In Costa Rica, the species is a common winter resident on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes, from lowlands to at least about 2,000 meters. It is especially associated with forest edges, broken forest, open areas, hillsides, savannas, and woodland clearings, and is less frequent in intact forest except in some parts of Guanacaste.
value.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, Broad-winged Hawks pass through mainly during fall migration from late September through mid-November, with especially notable movements along the Caribbean slope and highland routes. Spring migration generally occurs from early March through late May on both slopes. Many birds remain through the northern winter, making this one of Costa Rica’s most frequently observed wintering migratory raptors. Large flights may be seen soaring over ridges, valleys, and forested landscapes.
value.breeding: Breeding occurs mainly in large deciduous or mixed forests of Canada and the United States, not generally in Costa Rica. The nest is a loose platform of sticks, often placed in the lower or middle part of a large tree, commonly near a forest edge, road, water body, or opening. The clutch usually contains two or three eggs. Both adults participate in incubation and care of the young. Pairs are generally solitary and defend a nesting territory during the breeding season.
value.dietFeeding: The Broad-winged Hawk eats a varied diet of small mammals, frogs, snakes, lizards, insects, and occasionally small birds. It commonly hunts from a low or shaded perch, watching forest floors, roadside verges, grassy openings, and wet areas before dropping onto prey. In Costa Rica, wintering birds may forage along forest edges, in open woodland, and around clearings. Migrants may also take advantage of temporarily abundant insects and other prey during stopovers.
value.behavior: Broad-winged Hawks are often quiet and difficult to detect when perched inside forest, but they become conspicuous during migration. They use rising columns of warm air to travel efficiently and may gather in flocks numbering in the hundreds or thousands. In Costa Rica, individuals may be seen alone or in small groups during the winter, while major movements can produce broad streams of soaring birds. The species typically hunts from perches and roosts in trees or forest margins.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is considered stable to increasing, with increases documented in parts of the North American breeding range.
